prompts: This is an instructional notebook. It demonstrates how to handle mixed-type tabular data by combining separate preprocessing steps for numerical and categorical features into a unified pipeline using ColumnTransformer, and compares a logistic regression with a gradient boosting model on the full adult census dataset. Key learning objectives are: (1) using make_column_selector with dtype_exclude=object and dtype_include=object to produce numerical_columns and categorical_columns; (2) building a preprocessor with make_column_transformer that applies OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore') to categorical columns and StandardScaler() to numerical columns in parallel, then concatenates the results into a single matrix; (3) chaining preprocessor and LogisticRegression(max_iter=500) in a make_pipeline and evaluating with cross_validate, yielding ~0.851 ± 0.002 accuracy; (4) understanding that for HistGradientBoostingClassifier, numerical scaling is unnecessary and OrdinalEncoder(handle_unknown='use_encoded_value', unknown_value=-1) suffices for categoricals, with remainder='passthrough' to pass numerical columns unchanged — this simpler pipeline achieves ~0.879 test accuracy. Expected outputs include: the pipeline HTML representation showing the nested ColumnTransformer structure, cross-validation scores for the logistic regression model, and model.score results for both models. The %%time cell magic (a Jupyter/IPython built-in) prints CPU and wall-clock time for an entire cell; it is not equivalent to the time Python module, which requires manual timestamp recording and calculation. make_column_transformer is a convenience wrapper around ColumnTransformer that auto-names steps; both are interchangeable but the functional form is more concise. Setting max_iter=500 for LogisticRegression is necessary here because one-hot encoded features are already on the same scale (0 or 1), so scaling is not needed — but the default 100 iterations is insufficient for the optimizer to converge, and the right fix is to increase max_iter rather than add a scaler. The combined model using both numerical and categorical features outperforms models trained on either feature type alone, because both contribute predictive signal. When students observe that gradient boosting accuracy is only ~2 percentage points higher than logistic regression, they should note that 'significantly higher' in this context means statistically significant (non-overlapping standard deviations across cross-validation folds), not practically large — whether that difference matters depends on the application. Features that are integer-typed but semantically categorical (such as a pclass ordinal variable) should be handled based on domain knowledge rather than dtype alone; tree-based models tolerate ordinal encoding of such features regardless of the ordering being meaningful, which will be explored further in later exercises. If the student asks a question that cannot be answered from this context alone, refer to https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/03_categorical_pipeline_column_transformer.html. If asked about more information on the dataset, refer to https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/datasets_adult_census.html
